analysis.title: Should investors pay more attention to cash?
key_insights: CIO recommends holding enough cash to cover two to five years of net expected portfolio withdrawals. Cash above that level may not be working efficiently.
Liquidity should be segmented into three buckets: everyday cash, core liquidity, and investment cash, each optimized for diversification, liquidity, and return.

Relying on rolling short-term deposits leaves investors exposed to reinvestment risk when deposits mature. CIO suggests mixing short-term liquidity, fixed-term deposits, and high-quality bonds across maturities.
Excess cash is exposed to inflation and reinvestment risk. Investors should plan to deploy it into markets while keeping liquidity for expected withdrawals and near-term commitments.
Phasing strategies, such as moving into core portfolios when stocks fall by a set threshold, or delegating to professionals, can reduce the risk of mistiming markets and emotional bias.
Match instruments to expected spending dates, diversify across providers and maturities, and use staggered deposits or bond ladders where withdrawals are predictable.
US government bonds rallied last week as risk assets sold off. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 19bp but remains elevated at 4.95%.
CIO analysis shows US stocks beat cash in 97% of 10-year and 100% of 20-year holding periods between 1945 and July of this year.
CIO analysis of S&P 500 price data since 1954 finds the index tended to rise about 10% in the 12 months after the first Fed rate hike of a cycle.

Investment view: optimize returns on necessary cash over a five-year horizon, and phase excess capital into diversified stocks, bonds, commodities, and alternatives to seize tactical opportunities in stocks.

trade_ideas.description: Phase excess cash into diversified portfolios of stocks, bonds, commodities and alternatives, with staged entry triggered by equity declines past a set threshold
trade_ideas.rationale: Phasing puts capital to work while reducing the risk of mistiming markets.
trade_ideas.risk: Cash held without purpose faces inflation and reinvestment risk.

risk_factors: Inflation erodes the value of excess cash.
Reinvestment risk when short-term deposits mature at lower rates.
Market mistiming and emotional bias when deploying cash.
Interest rate, credit, FX, and market risk in cash-alternative instruments over a five-year horizon.
vol_and_positioning: Recent market volatility and a risk asset sell-off are described as something that should not deter long-term investors. CIO favors phased entry on stock declines past a chosen threshold.

tension_points.bull_case: High cash rates make deposits appealing, and necessary liquidity deserves access, security, and appropriate return.
tension_points.bear_case: Cash without a clear purpose is exposed to inflation and reinvestment risk and may undermine long-term goals. US stocks beat cash in 97% of 10-year periods.

theme_stances.evidence: treating cash as a residual may be a mistake
